newsitem.title: ITALY: FORECAST - Italy CPI seen averaging 2.9 pct in 1997.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Italy CPI seen averaging 2.9 pct in 1997.

text.p: Italian inflation, on a downward trend since the beginning of the year, is expected to average 3.9 percent in 1996 and 2.9 percent next year, a Reuter quarterly poll of 13 analysts showed.
"We are nearing levels which for Italy are exceptional," said Gianluca Sanna, economist at Banco di Sardegna in Milan.

The poll, carried out in the week of October 7, showed analysts on average expect fourth quarter 1996 consumer price inflation to drop to 3.0 percent year-on-year and then hold below that level for the whole of next year.
Latest government estimates see annual inflation at or under 3.0 percent by end-December for a 1996 average of 3.9 percent and with a targeted 1997 average of 2.5 percent.

CPI, at 5.8 percent at the end of December 1995, has fallen throughout this year to reach a 27-year low of 3.4 percent in August. The trend appeared to stall in September when the rate was unchanged, but further falls are seen in the last quarter.
"We have seen a very sharp deceleration in 1996 on a yearly basis. We started the year at 5.8 percent and we'll end it below three percent," said Daniele Castelnuovo of Euromobiliare.
"...we shall see a fall to below three percent in November and with a bit of luck we could see 2.7 or 2.8 percent in December," he said.

Sanna noted that September CPI had been "doped" by one-off hikes in soccer club ticket prices at the start of the new season. "But from October the downward trend will continue and we see 2.9 or 3.0 percent at end-December," he said.
However, analysts expressed some uncertainty over forecasting the inflation trend from January next year.

"From January, inflation won't see a marked, continued fall, it is more likely to show up and down fluctuations. The government's forecast for an average 1997 rate of 2.5 percent could be a bit hopeful," Sanna said.
Robert Prior, Italy economist at HSBC James Capel, agreed. He saw average inflation next year of 3.1 percent.
He saw December's year-on-year rate at 2.9 to 3.0 percent. "But from January onwards there is a bit of uncertainty with the economy seen remaining reasonably weak."

He cited a pickup in wage growth as likely impacting inflation. "The question is to what extent this will be absorbed by margins - perhaps not completely. The other pressure on inflation will be the effect of higher oil prices and Italy as a major crude importer is therefore vulnerable.
"So wages and oil prices make us a bit nervous about CPI continuing to fall back in 1997, but all in all it's a fairly neutral picture," Prior added.
Bank of Italy Governor Antonio Fazio has said the central bank's monetary policy was aimed at lowering the inflation rate "to enable a permanent lowering of structural interest rates."

He has indicated that a further key interest rate cut was dependent on inflation falling below three percent. The Bank last cut its discount rate in July to 8.25 percent from a 9.0 percent level unchanged since May 1995.
